meta.blurb: A duke must marry within a year or lose his land to a cousin who would sell every farm. Hester, a farmer's daughter quick with numbers, needs money to save her family. Her contract has three rules, and one is the truth.
meta.bible: Hester Penhallow: a farmer's daughter of about twenty-four from Little Ashby, quick with numbers and plain-spoken; becomes Duchess of Carrowmere. Alistair Vane: Duke of Carrowmere, about thirty, shy, proud and kind underneath; never read his own estate accounts. Carrowmere Park: the Duke's great house and estate in the English countryside. Little Ashby: the village where Hester lives. Josiah Penhallow: Hester's father, an honest farmer in debt; becomes the Steward. Wren: Hester's twelve-year-old sister, bright and opinionated. Rupert Vane: Alistair's charming cousin, who would inherit Carrowmere and sell its farms and cut its oak wood. Mr Quill: the family lawyer. Mr Gale: the Steward, who has stolen rents for Rupert. Mrs Dunn: the housekeeper. Lady Fenwick: Alistair's sharp-tongued aunt, who is kinder than she seems. Mr Holloway: an old tenant farmer whose mill wheel is broken. Sir Thomas Ashe: the Magistrate. River Carr: the river beside the Mill. Michaelmas: the autumn feast day, when the debt is due and the ball is held. The old Duke's will: the Duke must marry within a year or Rupert inherits. The Contract: a one-year marriage of convenience with three conditions set by Hester: her own rooms, a voice in the estate Accounts, and always the truth. Key words: Bailiff, Ledgers, Duke, Duchess, Tenants, Farmers, Sheep, Sandbags, Flood, Mill, Oak, Harvest, Vicar, Coronet, Primroses, Marble, Cousin, Farm, Library. Setting: England, 1818, an invented estate. Voice and tone: warm, witty, a little old-fashioned, romantic, with gentle comedy; no violence.

B1B2: Hester Penhallow keeps the accounts for her father's small farm in the village of Little Ashby. This morning a letter has come from the bailiff, and the family's debt must be paid by Michaelmas.
That afternoon a grand carriage breaks a wheel in the lane outside the farm. A tall, tired young man in an expensive coat climbs out into the mud and says a word he should not say.
While the wheel is mended, Alistair watches a young woman at the farm gate argue with the bailiff. She points out three mistakes in his sums, and the man turns red and says nothing.
At Carrowmere Park, the lawyer Mr Quill reads the will of Alistair's late grandfather. If Alistair does not marry within a year, the whole estate will pass to his cousin Rupert.
Alistair knows that Rupert would sell the tenants' farms and cut down the old oak wood for money. Yet he cannot bear the thought of marrying a stranger who only wants a title.
The next day Alistair rides to the farm and makes Hester an offer. She will marry him for one year, and in return he will pay her father's debts and her sister's school fees.
Hester is insulted and tells him exactly what she thinks of a man who buys a wife like a horse. Alistair leaves the garden red in the face, and he does not argue.
That night a second letter comes from Wren's school, asking for the unpaid fees. Hester looks at her little sister asleep and decides that pride is too expensive.
Hester rides to Carrowmere Park and says yes, but she has three conditions. She will have her own room, a voice in the estate accounts, and the truth from him at all times.
The wedding is held in the little church at Little Ashby, with only a handful of guests. Hester's father weeps, Wren grins, and the vicar speaks so quickly that it is over in ten minutes.

Carrowmere Park is the largest house Hester has ever seen, with a hundred windows and a floor of cold white stone. The servants line up in the hall and stare at their new Duchess as if she were a ghost.
Mrs Dunn, the kind and sharp-eyed housekeeper, shows Hester to her own set of rooms. Hester then asks to see the estate's accounts, and she is led to a dusty room full of untouched ledgers.
Lady Fenwick, Alistair's sharp-tongued aunt, arrives for tea and studies Hester through a small glass. She asks how and where the couple met, and she does not seem to believe a word of the answers.

At dinner Hester and Alistair invent a romantic story about their first meeting, with a storm and a runaway horse. They keep straight faces until Lady Fenwick leaves, and then they laugh until they cry.
After a week of study, Hester finds that a large part of the farm rents never reached the estate's bank. Every missing page is in the handwriting of Mr Gale, the steward.
Hester tells Alistair what she has found, and he goes pale. He admits that he has never once read the accounts, and he asks her, humbly, to teach him how.
They work together until midnight, night after night, and Alistair learns quickly. He makes tea for them both, and it tastes so terrible that Hester laughs until she cannot breathe.
Hester and Alistair drive a pony cart to visit each tenant farm on the estate. The farmers are shy of the Duke, but they warm to Hester, who knows about crops and animals.
Old Mr Holloway takes Alistair to the mill and shows him the great wheel, which has been broken for three years. Alistair listens carefully and promises that it will be mended by winter.
Cousin Rupert arrives unannounced with a charming smile and a carriage full of expensive presents. He kisses Hester's hand and congratulates them both, but his eyes keep moving around the house.
Later Rupert finds Hester alone and offers her a bag of gold if she will leave her husband. She gives the bag back to him and tells him that she is not for sale.
That evening Hester keeps her promise and tells Alistair everything that Rupert said. Alistair is quiet for a long time, and then he thanks her for her honesty.
At the harvest supper in the village barn, the fiddlers play and everyone dances. Hester steps on the Duke's foot twice, and the farmers cheer louder each time.
After the dance they sit on a cart under the stars, and Alistair talks about his father. The old man never smiled, and Alistair is afraid that he will be just the same.
Hester tells him about her mother, who taught her to love numbers and died when she was fifteen. They sit quietly together and realise that they have become real friends.
In a locked drawer in Mr Gale's office, Hester finds a letter in Rupert's handwriting. It thanks Gale for the money and tells him to keep quiet until the year is over.
Alistair wants to throw Mr Gale out at once, but Hester persuades him to wait. They need proof that no court could doubt, so she copies every figure into a small notebook.
One night a terrible storm breaks over Carrowmere, and the River Carr starts to rise. A boy rides in from the mill to say that the water is nearly over the bank.
Alistair and Hester ride out in the pouring rain and lead the tenants through the night. They move the sheep to high ground and build a wall of sandbags in front of the mill.
At dawn the water begins to fall, and the mill is safe. Alistair and Hester sit on a wall, covered in mud and laughing, and then he kisses her and she kisses him back.
Suddenly Hester steps away, her hand over her mouth, and reminds him of their contract. Alistair looks hurt, but he nods and lets her go.
For many days they speak only about the weather and the accounts, and they are painfully polite. Both of them are miserable, but neither knows how to begin.
Lady Fenwick takes Hester's arm in the garden and says she is not a fool. She says that she has not seen her nephew smile like this since he was a small boy.
That night Hester cannot sleep, because she has no title and no fortune. She is afraid that he only feels grateful, and that gratitude is not the same as love.
The Michaelmas ball at Carrowmere Park is the grandest evening of the year, and the whole county has come. Hester walks down the staircase in blue silk, and Alistair forgets how to speak.
Halfway through the evening Rupert stands on a chair and holds up a paper. It is a copy of the marriage contract, and he tells the whole room that the Duchess is nothing but a hired wife.
The room falls silent, and every face turns to look at Hester. Alistair, shocked, cannot find a single word, and so she lifts her skirts and walks out through the doors.
At last Alistair finds his voice and tells the ballroom the truth. He shows them Hester's notebook, which proves that Rupert and Mr Gale have been stealing, and Sir Thomas orders them held.
As soon as the guests understand, Alistair runs out to the stable and saddles his fastest horse. He rides through the pouring rain to Little Ashby without his coat or his hat.
He finds Hester in her father's kitchen, sitting by the stove with a cup of tea she has not touched. He stands dripping on the floor and says that he is sorry for his silence.
Hester says quietly that she is tired of being convenient. She does not want to be a useful wife, she tells him, but a wife who is truly chosen.
Alistair says that he loves her, and that he has done so since the day of the flood. He takes the contract from his pocket and drops it into the stove.
Hester says that she loves him too, and she has been afraid to say it. They kiss by the warm stove, while Wren watches round the door and giggles.
In the morning they drive back to Carrowmere Park in the farm cart. The tenants line the drive, with old Mr Holloway at the front, and they cheer for their Duke and their Duchess.
Alistair keeps his promise and has the old mill wheel mended. He also asks Josiah Penhallow, Hester's father, to be the new steward of the estate, and the old man cries.
Rupert is made to repay everything that he stole, and Mr Gale loses his post. Alistair shows mercy and does not send his cousin to prison, but Rupert must leave the country.
Wren comes to live at Carrowmere Park and goes to a good school in the nearby town. She decides that the library is the best room in the world.
In the spring they marry again in the little church at Little Ashby, and this time the whole village is invited. Hester walks up the aisle on her father's arm, and Alistair is not afraid of anything.
One evening they walk hand in hand through the old oak wood that Rupert wanted to cut down. Hester says that she intends to keep the estate's books for the rest of her life.
A year to the day after the first contract, Alistair gives Hester a small folded paper. It has only one line on it, which says that this marriage is forever, with no conditions.
C1C2: In the kitchen of the small farm at Little Ashby, Hester Penhallow bent over her father's accounts, as she had done every evening since her mother's death. The morning's letter from the bailiff lay open beside her candle, and it demanded that a heavy debt be settled by Michaelmas or the farm would be sold. She was a woman who could make any sum balance, but no arithmetic in the world could find money that was not there.

That afternoon a magnificent black carriage lost a wheel in the rutted lane outside the farm and settled sideways into the mud with a groan. A tall young man in an exquisite coat climbed out, surveyed the damage, and muttered a word that no duke ought to know. This was Alistair Vane, Duke of Carrowmere, who had been travelling all day and was in no mood to be inconvenienced by a lane.

While the wheel was being mended, Alistair noticed a young woman at the gate quarrelling with a stout bailiff over a long column of figures. She found three errors in his reckoning in as many minutes, and delivered the verdict in a voice so calm that the man turned crimson and fell silent. The Duke, who had never in his life seen anyone win an argument with arithmetic, stood in the lane and stared.

At Carrowmere Park that evening, the lawyer Mr Quill unfolded the will of the late Duke and read it aloud in a dry, careful voice. The old man had decreed that his grandson must be married within a year of his death, or the whole estate, house, farms and woodland, would pass to his other grandson, Rupert Vane. Alistair listened with the stillness of a man hearing the sentence of a court.

From the library window Alistair gazed at the tenant farms and the ancient oak wood that Rupert would certainly sell for profit within a month. Yet he could not bring himself to court some society girl who would smile at his rank and ignore the man, and he had no wish to be loved for a coronet. There had to be another way, he thought, and there was only one that he could see.

The next morning Alistair rode to the Penhallow farm, took off his hat in the garden, and laid his offer before Hester like a merchant presenting terms. She would marry him for one year and bear his name, and in return he would clear her father's debts and pay for her sister's schooling, and at the end she would be free. He said it all so plainly and so politely that for a moment she failed to grasp that he was asking for a wife.

Hester, who had been called many things but never a bargain, informed him exactly what she thought of men who purchased wives as though they were horses. Alistair, scarlet to the tips of his ears, bowed, apologised for the insult he had not intended, and retreated to his carriage without a word of argument. She slammed the gate behind him, and then stood shaking with fury in the middle of the path.

That night a second letter arrived, from the school where her twelve-year-old sister Wren was studying on borrowed time, demanding the fees that were months overdue. Hester stood beside the sleeping child, thought of the bailiff, the debt and the closed doors she would face, and weighed her pride against the girl's whole future. By the time the cock crowed the next morning, pride had lost the argument, though it had put up a magnificent fight.

Hester presented herself at Carrowmere Park in her best bonnet and informed the Duke that she would accept, subject to three conditions. She would have her own rooms, a genuine voice in the management of the estate's accounts, and complete honesty between them at all times, even when it was awkward. Alistair, after a moment of visible astonishment, agreed to every term, and Mr Quill drew up the contract that very afternoon.

The wedding took place in the small village church at Little Ashby, with Hester's father, Wren, Mr Quill and the housekeeper as the only witnesses. Alistair spoke his vows in a clear, careful voice, and Hester spoke hers rather faster, as though they were lines in a play she hoped to forget. When the vicar pronounced them married, the new Duchess felt nothing except a faint, unfamiliar dizziness.

Carrowmere Park rose before her like a palace of honey-coloured stone, with a hundred windows glittering and an entrance hall as cold and echoing as a cathedral. Rows of servants stood along the marble floor in perfect silence, studying their new Duchess with a curiosity they were too well trained to show. Hester lifted her chin and walked down the line, nodding to each in turn, because she could think of nothing else to do.

Mrs Dunn, the housekeeper, a stout and sharp-eyed woman with a ring of keys at her waist, conducted Hester to a handsome suite of rooms at the end of a long corridor. Hester thanked her, and then, to the housekeeper's evident surprise, asked to be shown the estate's accounts, and was taken to a dim chamber where dozens of ledgers lay under a thick blanket of dust. Before the housekeeper had finished apologising for the state of the room, the new Duchess had rolled up her sleeves and begun to dust.

Alistair's aunt, Lady Fenwick, swept in the following week for tea, and examined her new niece through a small gold-rimmed glass with the thoroughness of a customs officer. She asked precisely when, where and how the couple had met, and received answers so nervous and so contradictory that her eyebrows rose a quarter of an inch with each one. It was clear that she suspected something, though she was far too polite to say so aloud.

At dinner that evening the pair embroidered a story of their first meeting, complete with a thunderstorm, a bolting horse and a heroic rescue, each adding some absurd detail while Lady Fenwick looked on in frozen politeness. They managed to keep solemn faces until the old lady had retired to bed, and then Alistair put his head in his hands and wheezed with laughter. It was the first time Hester had seen him look anything other than weary and grave, and it made him look suddenly his age.

After a week among the ledgers, Hester discovered that a substantial portion of the tenants' rents had never reached the estate's bank, vanishing quietly into small, ingeniously disguised entries. Every one of the doubtful pages was in the neat handwriting of Mr Gale, the steward, who had come to the estate on Rupert's recommendation. She closed the book very gently, as one might close the door on a sleeping animal.

When Hester laid her discovery before him, Alistair went pale, and then he admitted, with a candour that cost him dearly, that he had never once opened the estate's books. He had left everything to Mr Gale and to the stewards before him, he said, and he was heartily ashamed of it. Then he drew up a chair beside hers and asked, quite humbly, whether she would teach him.

Night after night they worked side by side in the candlelit ledger room, and Alistair proved a quicker pupil than either of them had expected. At midnight he insisted on making tea himself, to prove that a Duke could do something useful, and produced a brew so appalling that Hester laughed until she had to put her head on the desk. Somewhere in that helpless laughter, though neither of them noticed, the strict rules of their contract quietly began to loosen.

Each morning that week the pair drove out in a pony cart to call upon the tenant farmers, who had not seen their Duke in years and did not know how to receive him. Hester, who understood crops and drainage and the price of a good ram, put them at ease within minutes, and the farmers' wives pressed jars of honey into her hands. Alistair, sitting beside her with the reins loose in his hands, watched her with an expression that she was too busy to notice.

Old Mr Holloway led the Duke to the mill on the River Carr and showed him the great wheel, split and silent after three winters of neglect. Without the mill, he said, half the farms must carry their grain eight miles to market, and no one had listened to him when he asked for help. Alistair listened to every word, and made a promise that he intended to keep.

Without warning, Alistair's cousin Rupert Vane arrived at Carrowmere Park in a glossy carriage laden with expensive gifts, smiling like a man who had never harboured an unkind thought. He kissed Hester's hand, praised the marriage in the most flowery terms, and congratulated the Duke on his remarkable luck. His eyes, however, kept wandering over the walls and the furniture as though he were pricing everything in the house.

Later that afternoon Rupert found Hester alone in the garden room and murmured that a clever woman might prefer a comfortable sum of money to a cold marriage. He placed a heavy purse in her lap, and waited with a pleasant smile for her to be sensible. Hester returned it to him with perfect courtesy, remarking that she had already been offered a bargain once and had no wish to be offered another.

That evening, remembering the third of her conditions, Hester told Alistair everything that had passed between her and his cousin, including the purse and the polite smile. Alistair was silent for a long while, a muscle moving in his jaw, and then he thanked her in a voice that was not quite steady. No one, he said, had ever refused anything so tempting on his behalf, and he did not yet know how to thank her for it.

The harvest supper was held in the great barn at Little Ashby, with fiddlers on a hay cart and a hundred lanterns swinging from the beams. Hester, who had never learned the fashionable steps, trod twice on the Duke's foot during the first dance, while the farmers roared their approval with every stumble. Alistair, who had been taught dancing by the finest masters in England, did not seem to mind a single bruise.

Afterwards they sat on the tailboard of a cart beneath a sky crowded with stars, and Alistair spoke about his father, a proud, cold man who had hardly ever spoken a kind word to his son. He confessed that he had always feared the same hardness lay hidden in himself, waiting for the right moment to appear. Hester told him, with absolute conviction, that a hard man did not mend a mill for an old farmer.

In return Hester told him about her mother, who had taught her to love arithmetic at the kitchen table and who had died when Hester was only fifteen. The words came more easily than she had expected, and Alistair listened without interrupting, simply being there beside her. When they finally walked home through the dark lane, both of them understood that the word friend now described them better than the word contract.

In a locked drawer in the steward's office, which Hester opened with a hairpin and a clear conscience, they found a letter in Rupert's flowing hand. It thanked Mr Gale warmly for the sums he had sent, instructed him to keep the books quiet until the year was over, and promised him a handsome reward when the estate changed hands. Alistair read it twice, slowly, and by the end of the second reading the colour had drained from his face.

Alistair wished to dismiss Mr Gale that very hour, but Hester, who understood the difference between anger and evidence, begged him to wait. A court would need figures, dates and witnesses, she said, and they must gather them all before either man suspected that he was watched. For the next fortnight she copied columns of numbers into a small black notebook, which she kept beneath her pillow.

One October night a terrible storm broke over Carrowmere, and rain hammered the windows as though it meant to break through the glass. Near midnight a boy on a lathered pony clattered into the yard with news that the River Carr was rising fast and would soon overflow the lower fields and the mill. Alistair was already pulling on his boots and shouting for lanterns and ropes before the breathless lad had finished speaking.

In the downpour Alistair and Hester rode out together and took command of a frightened, shivering crowd of tenants, whom they set to work with lanterns and shovels. The sheep were driven to the high pasture, a long wall of sandbags rose before the mill, and the Duke himself stood waist deep in cold water, passing sacks along the line. Hester, in a borrowed coat and mud to her knees, shouted orders that everyone, including the Duke, obeyed without a murmur of protest.

By dawn the river had turned back, the mill stood unharmed, and the whole company sat down on the wet grass, too exhausted even to cheer. Alistair and Hester, filthy and soaked, found themselves side by side on a low stone wall, laughing helplessly at the state of one another, until the laughter faded and he kissed her. She kissed him back, with an eagerness and a tenderness that astonished them both, and for a long moment the whole sleeping valley seemed to hold its breath.

Then, abruptly, Hester drew back and pressed a hand over her mouth, as though she had broken something precious that could never be mended. She reminded him in a trembling voice that they had signed a contract, and that a contract was no foundation for what she had just done. Alistair, who had never in his life forced anything on anyone, bowed his head and let her walk away.

For the following week they spoke to each other with an elaborate courtesy that would have done credit to two ambassadors at a funeral. They discussed the weather, the mill and the price of wheat, and each sat at the opposite end of the long breakfast table, miserably studying a boiled egg. Even the footmen noticed the chill, and by the end of the week the servants' hall was humming with rival theories about what had gone wrong.

Lady Fenwick drew Hester's arm through her own in the garden and announced, without preamble, that she was not a fool and had never been one. She had known from the first evening that the marriage began as a bargain, she said, but she had not seen her nephew smile so freely since he was a small boy, and she knew the cause. Hester stared down at the gravel path for a long moment, entirely speechless, while a blackbird sang in the hedge as though nothing had happened.

That night Hester could not sleep, and she stood at her window turning the old aunt's words over and over, afraid to trust them. She had no title, no fortune and no polish, she told herself, and a man might easily mistake gratitude for love when he had been rescued from his own inheritance. It seemed safer to remain a convenient wife than to risk becoming a foolish one.

The Michaelmas ball at Carrowmere Park was the grandest evening of the year, and the whole county had assembled beneath the blazing chandeliers, from the magistrate Sir Thomas Ashe down to the humblest tenant. Hester descended the great staircase in a gown of blue silk that Lady Fenwick had insisted upon, and the music seemed to falter for a moment. Alistair, waiting at the foot of the stairs, entirely forgot the speech he had prepared.

In the middle of the evening Rupert climbed onto a chair, tapped his glass for silence, and held up a folded paper that he had bought from Mr Quill's clerk. It was a copy of the marriage contract, he announced, and it proved to the whole county that the new Duchess of Carrowmere was nothing more than a hired wife. A gasp ran around the ballroom like a wave, and several ladies pressed their fans to their lips in horror.

For a long moment nobody in the ballroom moved, and every eye in the county turned to Hester, who had gone as white as her gloves. Alistair, struck dumb by the cruelty of it, could not find one word to say, and in that dreadful pause she gathered her skirts and walked out through the tall doors with her head held high. The silence she left behind seemed to press upon the chandeliers, and it was worse than any noise.

At last Alistair found his voice, and it rang through the ballroom like a bell. He admitted that the contract was real, then held up Hester's black notebook and proved, page by page, that his cousin and the steward had been stealing from his tenants, and that the lady they mocked had discovered it. Sir Thomas Ashe rose from his seat and ordered both men to be held until morning.

The moment the guests had grasped the truth, Alistair strode from the ballroom, saddled his fastest horse with his own hands, and galloped toward Little Ashby through a night of lashing rain. He had no coat and no hat and no clear idea of what to say, but he knew with perfect certainty where she would have gone. Behind him, the bright windows of Carrowmere Park dwindled slowly to a faint gold smudge, and then the dark lane swallowed them entirely.

He found her in her father's kitchen, sitting beside the stove in her ruined ballgown, with a cup of tea going cold in her hands. Alistair stood dripping on the flagstones and told her that his silence in the ballroom had been the worst failure of his life, and that he would spend years making up for it if she allowed. She did not answer him at once, but she did not tell him to leave, and that, for the moment, was enough to keep him standing there.

“I am tired of being convenient,” Hester said at last, her voice low and steady. She had been useful all her life, she told him, to her father, to her sister, to the estate and to the contract, and she could not bear to be merely useful to a man she loved. She wanted, just once, to be chosen for herself, and not for the sums she could do.

“I choose you,” Alistair said, and the words came out rough and certain, as if they had been waiting a long time. He confessed that he had loved her since before the flood, since the first laughing evening in the ledger room, perhaps since the moment she corrected a bailiff at a farm gate. Then he drew the contract from his pocket, opened the stove door, and fed the paper to the flames.

Hester watched the paper curl, blacken and vanish, and then she told him, in a voice that wobbled with laughter and tears, that she loved him too and had been dreadfully afraid to say so. This time, neither of them remembered any contract, and the kiss that followed was long and unhurried and entirely theirs. From behind the door, Wren, who had been listening at the keyhole for at least ten minutes, let out a squeak so delighted that it gave her away completely.

They returned to Carrowmere Park the next morning in the farm cart, mud-spattered and sleepless and incandescently happy, to find the entire drive lined with tenants. Old Mr Holloway stood at their head, his cap in his hand, and led a roar of cheering for the Duke and Duchess that startled the rooks out of the elms. Hester, who had expected whispers and stares, found that she could not stop crying.

Before the first frost, the great wheel was mended and turning again, and the old miller wept openly as the first sacks of flour went through. Alistair also offered Josiah Penhallow, Hester's father, the position of steward, in recognition of a lifetime of honest farming and a daughter with a gift for sums. The old man accepted at once, then asked whether he might have a minute to blow his nose.

Rupert, shaken and subdued, was made to repay every shilling that he and Mr Gale had taken, and the steward was dismissed in disgrace. Alistair, who had once feared that he possessed his father's hardness, chose mercy over revenge and allowed his cousin to sail abroad rather than face a prison. It was, Hester told him, exactly the kind of strength that a hard man did not have.

Wren arrived at Carrowmere Park with a single trunk and a look of dazed delight, and was installed in a bright room overlooking the oak wood. She was sent to an excellent school in the nearby town, where her fees were paid in full and her opinions, to her teachers' dismay, were as firm as her sister's. Within a week she had claimed the library for her own, and was lecturing the footmen on the importance of proper arithmetic.

In the spring they were married a second time in the village church at Little Ashby, and on this occasion the pews were crammed with tenants, farmers' wives and wide-eyed children. Hester walked up the aisle on her father's arm with a bunch of wild primroses, and Alistair, waiting at the altar, was so happy that he forgot his vows entirely. The vicar had to prompt him twice, and nobody in the whole crowded church minded in the least.

One evening they strolled hand in hand beneath the vast oaks that Rupert had once planned to fell, whose new leaves made a green and golden roof above their heads. Hester remarked that she intended to keep the estate's ledgers for the rest of her life, and Alistair, who now read them himself, replied that he wished for nothing better. They walked on slowly through the green light, in no hurry whatever to reach the house, and the evening seemed to grow longer for their sake.

A year to the day after they had signed the first contract, Alistair handed Hester a small folded paper beside the fire, with an expression of mock solemnity. It contained a single line, in his own untidy hand, promising a marriage for the whole of their lives, with no terms, no conditions and no way out. Hester read it, laughed, took up the pen and signed her name with a flourish.
